sentence.en: I am learning German {{BLANK}} I want to work in Germany.

explanation.en:
„weil“ gives a reason, the verb goes to the end of the clause.
„dass“ introduces a fact, not a reason.
„wenn“ would be temporal or conditional, not causal.

sentence.en: She is not coming to work today {{BLANK}} she is sick.

explanation.en:
„weil“ fits here because a reason for the absence is given.
„obwohl“ would express a contrast (she comes despite being sick).
„ob“ introduces an indirect question.

sentence.en: He likes to help me {{BLANK}} we are good friends.

explanation.en:
„weil“ gives the reason why he helps; the verb „sind“ goes at the end.
„dass“ would only add a fact, not provide a reason.

sentence.en: Why were you late? – {{BLANK}} the bus didn't stop.

explanation.en:
As an answer to a „Why?“ question, the sentence often starts directly with „Weil“ (capitalised, start of sentence).
„Dass“ and „Ob“ do not fit grammatically here.

sentence.en: I am glad {{BLANK}} you helped me on the first day.

explanation.en:
„weil“ gives the reason for the joy, with the verb „geholfen hast“ at the end.
„denn“ would also be possible, but then the verb stays in position 2, not at the end — here „weil“ with final verb position fits.

sentence.en: I think {{BLANK}} the weather will be nice tomorrow.

explanation.en:
After „glauben“ (to believe) a fact follows with „dass“, the verb goes at the end.
„weil“ would introduce a reason, not an opinion.

sentence.en: She said {{BLANK}} she is coming at 8 o'clock.

explanation.en:
After „sagen“ (to say) you report a fact with „dass“.
„ob“ would express uncertainty or a question.

sentence.en: We hope {{BLANK}} the exam is not too difficult.

explanation.en:
After „hoffen“ (to hope) a „dass“-clause follows with the verb at the end.
„wenn“ would introduce a condition, not a hope.

sentence.en: I think {{BLANK}} German is an interesting language.

explanation.en:
„finden“ in the sense of „to think“ introduces an opinion with „dass“.
„als“ only fits with comparisons or single past events.

sentence.en: It is important {{BLANK}} you arrive at work on time.

explanation.en:
„Es ist wichtig, dass …“ is a fixed A2 structure for statements about importance.
„ob“ would only fit with questions about possibility.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} it rains, I take the bus.

explanation.en:
„Wenn“ describes a repeated condition (every time it rains).
„Als“ would only be correct for a single event in the past.

sentence.en: I will call you {{BLANK}} I am at home.

explanation.en:
„wenn“ here expresses the future point in time.
„dass“ would add a fact, not a point in time.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} you have questions, you can call me.

explanation.en:
„Wenn“ here states a condition (in case you have questions).
„Ob“ only fits after verbs like „to ask“ or „to know“.

sentence.en: We go for a walk {{BLANK}} the sun is shining.

explanation.en:
„wenn“ fits for a general, repeated condition in the present tense.
„als“ would only be correct for a single past event.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} you are new in a city, you often need help.

explanation.en:
„Wenn“ describes a general situation that is always true.
„Als“ would only be correct for a specific, single event in the past.

sentence.en: The subway is faster {{BLANK}} the bus.

explanation.en:
After a comparative form („faster“), „than“ follows.
„wie“ (as) is only used for equality („as fast as“).

sentence.en: My room is just as big {{BLANK}} your room.

explanation.en:
For equality, „genauso … wie“ (just as … as) is used.
„als“ would express a difference (faster/bigger than).

sentence.en: In winter it is colder {{BLANK}} in summer.

explanation.en:
„kälter“ (colder) is a comparative, so „als“ follows.
„wie“ only fits with equality, not with a difference.

sentence.en: That is the {{BLANK}} way to the station. (short)

explanation.en:
With the definite article „der“ and „Weg“, you need the superlative with the -ste ending: „der kürzeste“.
„kürzer“ would only be the comparative (comparing two things).

sentence.en: This apartment is not as expensive {{BLANK}} the other one.

explanation.en:
With „nicht so … wie“ you express that something is less than something else.
„als“ does not fit here because no comparative (e.g. „more expensive“) is used.

sentence.en: I {{BLANK}} unfortunately not come today, I am sick.

explanation.en:
„können“ (can) here expresses ability/possibility (not possible due to illness).
„müssen“ would express an obligation, which does not fit the context.

sentence.en: Children {{BLANK}} be quiet at school.

explanation.en:
„müssen“ (must) expresses a rule/obligation.
„dürfen“ would express permission, not an obligation.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} I open the window, please?

explanation.en:
„dürfen“ (may) is the polite form for asking permission.
„müssen“ would express an obligation, not a request for permission.

sentence.en: He {{BLANK}} swim very well before.

explanation.en:
With „früher“ (before) you need the past tense: „konnte“ (not „kann“).
„durfte“ would be permission, not ability.

sentence.en: We {{BLANK}} go to the party yesterday, but we had no time.

explanation.en:
„wollten“ (past tense of „wollen“) expresses a wish in the past that was not fulfilled.
„mussten“ would express an obligation, not a wish.

sentence.en: The picture is hanging {{BLANK}} the wall. (position)

explanation.en:
For position (where?) the two-way preposition „an“ is used with dative: „an der Wand“.
„auf“ fits better with horizontal surfaces like a table.

sentence.en: He puts the chair {{BLANK}} the table. (direction)

explanation.en:
For direction (where to?) the two-way preposition „an“ is used with accusative: „an den Tisch“.
The difference to the previous example: here the chair moves somewhere.

sentence.en: We live {{BLANK}} the city centre.

explanation.en:
For a place where you are located, you use „in“ with dative: „in der Stadtmitte“.
„zu“ would only express a direction (movement towards it).

sentence.en: Go right {{BLANK}} the corner.

explanation.en:
The fixed phrase „an der Ecke“ (at the corner) describes a position when giving directions.
„auf“ would be unusual here, it does not fit with „Ecke“.

sentence.en: The shop is {{BLANK}} the station.

explanation.en:
„neben“ with dative describes a position directly beside something.
„zwischen“ would need two reference points (between X and Y).

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} you please help me?

explanation.en:
„Könnten“ (subjunctive II) sounds more polite than the simple „Können“.
For a polite request, the subjunctive II form is typical.

sentence.en: Excuse me, {{BLANK}} you tell me where the station is?

explanation.en: After „Entschuldigung“ (excuse me), „könnten Sie …“ is a very typical, polite way to ask for directions.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} you be so kind as to open the door?

explanation.en: The fixed, very polite phrase is „Wären Sie so freundlich …?“ (subjunctive II of „sein“).

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} you please show me the way?

explanation.en: „Können Sie mir bitte …?“ is a simple, everyday polite request at A2 level.

sentence.en: I would have a question, {{BLANK}} you have a moment.

explanation.en:
„wenn“ here introduces a polite condition (an indirect, subjunctive-like tone).
„ob“ would express uncertainty, not a condition.

sentence.en: He is wearing a red shirt.

explanation.en: After the indefinite article „ein“, neuter nouns in the nominative/accusative need the ending -es: „ein rotes Hemd“.

sentence.en: She buys green trousers.

explanation.en: After „eine“ (feminine, accusative), the adjective needs the ending -e: „eine grüne Hose“.

sentence.en: That is my new sweater.

explanation.en: After the possessive article „mein“, masculine nouns in the nominative need the ending -er: „mein neuer Pullover“.

sentence.en: I am looking for a comfortable chair.

explanation.en: After „einen“ (masculine, accusative), the adjective needs the ending -en: „einen bequemen Stuhl“.

sentence.en: We have a small room.

explanation.en: After „ein“ (neuter, accusative), the adjective needs the ending -es: „ein kleines Zimmer“.

sentence.en: He gets annoyed about the noise in the classroom.

explanation.en:
„sich“ is the reflexive pronoun for the third person singular in the accusative (er ärgert sich).
„ihn“ would mean a different object (he annoys someone else).

sentence.en: We are already really looking forward to the weekend.

explanation.en:
For „wir“ the reflexive pronoun in the accusative is „uns“.
„euch“ would be for „ihr“, „sich“ for the third person.

sentence.en: Do you already feel comfortable in the new class?

explanation.en:
For „du“ the reflexive pronoun in the accusative is „dich“, not „dir“ (dative).
„fühlen“ requires the accusative here.

sentence.en: Jonas is interested in natural sciences.

explanation.en:
The verb „sich interessieren“ requires the fixed preposition „für“ + accusative.
„an“ or „von“ do not fit grammatically here.

sentence.en: Cem often thinks of his school days in Turkey.

explanation.en:
„denken an“ + accusative is a fixed combination.
„denken über“ does not exist, „auf“ does not fit with „denken“.

sentence.en: Mr Klinke is annoyed about the noise in the classroom.

explanation.en:
„sich ärgern über“ + accusative is the fixed preposition for this expression.
„auf“ only fits with „sich freuen auf“.

sentence.en: The dispute has been going on for days, that's why she calls the property management.

explanation.en:
„deshalb“ (that's why) states a consequence, the verb comes right after it (position 2).
„weil“ would introduce a subordinate clause with the verb at the end.

sentence.en: She did not pass the exam, that's why she has to try again.

explanation.en:
After „deshalb“ the verb follows directly (main clause), it expresses a logical consequence.
„dass“ would introduce a subordinate clause, not an independent main clause.

sentence.en: The boss was unhappy with the work, that's why he organised a meeting.

explanation.en:
„deshalb“ stands at the start of the clause, followed directly by the conjugated verb „hat“.
„damit“ would express a purpose, not a consequence.

sentence.en: Could you please help me? I can't find the form.

explanation.en:
„Könnten“ (subjunctive II) sounds more polite than the simple „Können“.
For a polite request, the subjunctive II is typical.

sentence.en: I would advise you to do an internship first.

explanation.en:
„würde“ (subjunctive II of „werden“) makes the advice more polite and less direct.
„werde“ (present tense) would be too direct for advice.

sentence.en: Could you do me a favour and pick up the children?

explanation.en:
When making a request to someone you know (du), „Könntest“ is used for politeness.
„Kannst“ would be more neutral, less polite.

sentence.en: An honest apology would make the situation much easier.

explanation.en:
„würde“ here expresses a polite assumption/possibility (subjunctive II).
„wird“ (future/present) would be a certain statement, not a cautious assumption.

sentence.en: The chair that is made of wood has very good material.

explanation.en: After „ein“ (neuter, accusative: „Material“), the adjective needs the ending -es: „ein gutes Material“.

sentence.en: With the new battery, the phone works normally again.

explanation.en: After the preposition „mit“ (+ dative), the definite article for masculine takes the form „dem“: „mit dem neuen Akku“.

sentence.en: The useful app helps with learning German.

explanation.en: After the definite article „die“ (feminine, nominative), the adjective needs the ending -e: „die nützliche App“.

sentence.en: In the bright foreground, you can see a woman with a dog.

explanation.en: After „im“ (= in dem, dative, masculine), the adjective needs the ending -en: „im hellen Vordergrund“.

sentence.en: The saleswoman, who is very friendly, gives her a compliment.

explanation.en:
The relative pronoun refers to „die Verkäuferin“ (feminine) in the nominative: „die“.
„der“ would be for masculine, „das“ for neuter.

sentence.en: The salesman who works on the second floor knows a lot about music.

explanation.en:
The relative pronoun refers to „der Verkäufer“ (masculine) in the nominative: „der“.
„den“ would be the accusative, but here the relative pronoun is the subject of the clause.

sentence.en: The dress that is hanging in the shop window pleases her a lot.

explanation.en:
The relative pronoun refers to „das Kleid“ (neuter) in the nominative: „das“.
„dessen“ would be a genitive relative pronoun (possession), which does not fit here.

sentence.en: After her training, Elif will become a good craftswoman.

explanation.en:
„werden“ expresses a future change/development: „she becomes something“.
„ist“ would describe a current state, not a development.

sentence.en: What would you like to become if you could choose freely?

explanation.en:
„würdest“ (subjunctive II) fits the hypothetical question with „wenn du könntest“.
„wirst“ (present) would be for a real, non-hypothetical question.

sentence.en: Craft is becoming increasingly important in Germany.

explanation.en:
„wird … wichtiger“ describes a gradual change in the present.
„ist wichtiger“ would only express the current state without development.

sentence.en: She lets her son walk the dog alone.

explanation.en:
„lassen“ + infinitive means allowing someone to do something.
„machen“ would mean that she does it herself.

sentence.en: I have my car repaired at the workshop.

explanation.en:
„lassen“ + infinitive expresses that someone else does the work for you.
„machen“ would mean that you repair it yourself.

sentence.en: Do you let your son walk the dog alone?

explanation.en:
After „lassen“, the infinitive is used without „zu“: „lassen … ausführen“.
„auszuführen“ (with „zu“) would be wrong here.

sentence.en: She explains the rules precisely so that everyone understands them.

explanation.en:
„damit“ states the purpose of an action (two different subjects: she / everyone).
„dass“ would only add a fact, not a purpose.

sentence.en: He voluntarily helps at the animal shelter so that the animals get more attention.

explanation.en:
„damit“ here expresses the purpose of his help.
„weil“ would give a reason, not a goal for the future.

sentence.en: The parents give him more responsibility so that he becomes more independent.

explanation.en:
„damit“ states the desired result (goal) of the parents' action.
„ob“ would express uncertainty, not a goal.

sentence.en: I don't know where the responsible office is located.

explanation.en:
In an indirect question with a question word (where?), „wo“ comes directly at the start of the clause.
„ob“ would only be used for yes/no questions.

sentence.en: She asks whether her foreign driving licence is valid in Germany.

explanation.en:
For a yes/no question without a question word, the subordinate clause uses „ob“.
„wo“ or „wann“ would need a specific question word.

sentence.en: He asks which authority is responsible for his application.

explanation.en:
„welche“ (which) asks about a choice (which of several authorities) and stands at the start of the clause.
„ob“ does not fit here because it is not a yes/no question.

sentence.en: Nobody knows whether you can appeal against a fine notice.

explanation.en:
Since the question can be answered with yes/no (Is it possible?), „ob“ is used.
„wo“ or „wann“ would ask about place or time, not possibility.

sentence.en: The company writes that her application has arrived.

explanation.en:
After „schreiben“ (to write) you report a fact with „dass“, verb at the end.
„ob“ would express uncertainty, but here it is a certain statement.

sentence.en: He hopes that the training will be fun for him.

explanation.en:
After „hoffen“ (to hope) a „dass“-clause follows with the verb at the end.
„als“ only fits with single events in the past.

sentence.en: You notice immediately that a lot of work is done in this workshop.

explanation.en:
„merken, dass …“ (to notice that) is a fixed structure for stating an observation as a fact.
„wie“ would ask about the manner, not the fact itself.

sentence.en: We are celebrating tonight, although we have to get up early tomorrow.

explanation.en:
„obwohl“ (although) expresses a contrast (celebrating despite having to get up early).
„weil“ would give a reason, which does not make sense here.

sentence.en: She sends the invitations early so that everyone can plan in time.

explanation.en:
„damit“ states the purpose of sending them early.
„weil“ would give a reason, but here it is about a purpose for the future.

sentence.en: We invite all the neighbours because we have a good relationship with them.

explanation.en:
„weil“ gives the reason for the invitation.
„damit“ would express a purpose, but here a reason is given.

sentence.en: This tradition has existed for a long time, although many young people no longer know it.

explanation.en:
„obwohl“ (although) expresses a contrast (the tradition exists anyway, although it is becoming unknown).
„wenn“ would express a condition or time, not a contrast.

We use Perfekt to talk about past actions. It is formed using haben or sein in the 2nd position and the Partizip II at the very end of the sentence.
Example: Ich habe Deutsch gelernt. Er ist nach Berlin geflogen.

rule.en:
Formation: haben or sein in position 2 + Partizip II (past participle) at the end of the sentence.

ichhabe / bin
duhast / bist
er/sie/eshat / ist
wirhaben / sind
ihrhabt / seid
sie/Siehaben / sind

Forming the Partizip II:
• regular verbs: ge + stem + t → machen → gemacht
• irregular verbs: ge + stem + en (often with a vowel change) → fahren → gefahren
• verbs ending in -ieren: no ge- → studieren → studiert
• separable verbs: prefix + ge + stem → einkaufen → eingekauft
• inseparable verbs (be-, ge-, er-, ver-, zer-, ent-, emp-, miss-): no ge- → verstehen → verstanden

sein or haben?
sein: motion (gehen, fahren, fliegen), change of state (aufwachen, sterben) + the verbs sein, werden, bleiben.
haben: all other verbs, all reflexive verbs, and all verbs with an accusative object.

Examples:
Ich habe einen Brief geschrieben. (I have written a letter.)
Er ist nach Hause gegangen. (He has gone home.)

explanation.en:
Präteritum is another past tense. At the A2 level, we mostly use it only for war (to be) and hatte (to have).
Example: Letztes Jahr war ich in Deutschland und hatte viel Zeit.

rule.en:
Formation of regular verbs: stem + -te + ending.

ichmachte
dumachtest
er/sie/esmachte
wirmachten
ihrmachtet
sie/Siemachten

Irregular verbs change their stem vowel (Ablaut) and often have their own forms, e.g. fahren → fuhr, gehen → ging — these must be learned individually.

Important for A2: In everyday speech, the Perfekt is usually used. But sein, haben and modal verbs are almost always used in the Präteritum.

seinhaben
ichwarhatte
duwarsthattest
er/sie/eswarhatte
wirwarenhatten
ihrwarthattet
sie/Siewarenhatten

Example: Letztes Jahr war ich in Deutschland und hatte viel Zeit. (Last year I was in Germany and had a lot of time.)

explanation.en:
Modal verbs (können, müssen, wollen, dürfen, sollen, mögen) change their form and sit in the 2nd position. The main verb goes to the end of the sentence in its infinitive form.
Note: 'ich' and 'er/sie/es' forms are identical (ich kann, er kann).

rule.en:
Position: the modal verb is in position 2 and is conjugated. The second (main) verb is in the Infinitiv right at the end of the sentence.

Personkönnen
ichkann
dukannst
er/sie/eskann
wirkönnen
ihrkönnt
sie/Siekönnen

Conjugated the same way:
• müssen → muss, musst, muss, müssen, müsst, müssen
• wollen → will, willst, will, wollen, wollt, wollen
• dürfen → darf, darfst, darf, dürfen, dürft, dürfen
• sollen → soll, sollst, soll, sollen, sollt, sollen
• mögen → mag, magst, mag, mögen, mögt, mögen

Note: for all modal verbs (except sollen), the forms for ich and er/sie/es are identical, and the stem vowel often changes in the singular.

Example: Ich kann gut schwimmen. (I can swim well.) Wir müssen jetzt gehen. (We have to go now.)

title.en: Modal verbs in the simple past

explanation.en:
In the past tense, modal verbs lose their umlauts (ä, ö, ü) and add '-te-'.
Example: können -> ich konnte, müssen -> ich musste, wollen -> ich wollte.

rule.en:
Formation: in the Präteritum, modal verbs lose their umlaut (ä, ö, ü → a, o, u) and take the ending -te, like regular verbs.

InfinitivPräteritum (ich)
könnenkonnte
müssenmusste
wollenwollte
dürfendurfte
sollensollte
mögenmochte

Other persons (example können): du konntest, er/sie/es konnte, wir konnten, ihr konntet, sie/Sie konnten.

Example: Als Kind konnte ich nicht schwimmen. (As a child I couldn't swim.) Ich musste jeden Tag früh aufstehen. (I had to get up early every day.)

explanation.en:
The conjunction weil answers the question 'Why?'. In a weil-clause, the conjugated verb moves to the very end of the sentence.
Example: Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Deutschland leben möchte.

rule.en:
Word order: main clause, + weil + subject + (further details) + ... + verb (conjugated, right at the end).

PositionweilSubjectDetailsVerb
Exampleweilichin Deutschlandlebe

Note: with two verbs (e.g. modal verb + infinitive or Perfekt), both verbs go together at the end of the sentence, with the conjugated verb absolutely last.

Examples:
Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Deutschland leben möchte. (I'm learning German because I want to live in Germany.)
Sie ist müde, weil sie viel gearbeitet hat. (She's tired because she worked a lot.)

explanation.en:
The conjunction dass connects clauses after verbs of thinking, saying, or feeling (glauben, sagen, wissen). The conjugated verb goes to the end.
Example: Ich weiß, dass du recht hast.

rule.en:
Word order: exactly like weil — after dass, the conjugated verb goes right to the end of the subordinate clause.

Use: dass connects a main clause with a subordinate clause after verbs of thinking, saying, or feeling.

Verbs with dass
glauben, denken, meinen (believe, think)
sagen, erzählen, antworten (say, tell, answer)
wissen, finden, hoffen (know, find, hope)
froh sein, sicher sein (be glad, be sure)

Examples:
Ich weiß, dass du recht hast. (I know that you're right.)
Er sagt, dass er morgen kommt. (He says that he's coming tomorrow.)

explanation.en:
We use wenn for conditions (If...) or repeated actions in the present/past. The verb goes to the end.
Example: Wenn es regnet, bleibe ich zu Hause.

rule.en:
Word order: wenn + subject + ... + verb (end). The main clause afterward often begins directly with the verb (the subordinate clause occupies position 1).

Two meanings:
1) Condition (If... then): Wenn es regnet, bleibe ich zu Hause. (If it rains, I stay home.)
2) Repetition in the present/past (= every time): Wenn ich Zeit habe, lese ich. (Whenever I have time, I read.)

Subordinate clauseMain clause
Wenn es regnet,bleibe ich zu Hause.

Note: right after the comma comes the verb (verb-subject inversion), because the subordinate clause takes up position 1 in the main clause.

explanation.en:
For single past events we use als, for repeated past events we use wenn. Schon means already (sooner/more than expected), erst means only/not until (later/less).
Example: Als ich Kind war, war ich erst einmal in Berlin.

rule.en:
als vs. wenn (past tense):
alsa single event in the past
wenna repeated event in the past (= every time)

Examples:
Als ich 18 war, habe ich meinen Führerschein gemacht. (once — When I was 18, I got my driver's license.)
Wenn ich früher Ferien hatte, bin ich immer zu meiner Oma gefahren. (several times — Whenever I had vacation, I always went to my grandma's.)

schon vs. erst:
schonearlier / more than expected (already)
erstlater / less than expected, not quite yet (only, just)

Examples:
Es ist schon 20 Uhr! (It's already 8pm! — that's late)
Es ist erst 8 Uhr. (It's only 8am. — that's early)
Ich war schon dreimal in Berlin. (I've already been to Berlin three times.) / Ich war erst einmal in Berlin. (I've only been to Berlin once.)

explanation.en:
Some verbs always require an object in the dative case (Question: To whom?). Key verbs: helfen, danken, gefallen, gehören, schmecken.
Example: Ich helfe dem Mann (Masculine: der -> dem).

rule.en:
Question: To whom? — these verbs always take an object in the Dativ (dative case), never the accusative.

VerbMeaning
helfento help
dankento thank
gefallento please/like
gehörento belong to
schmeckento taste (good)
gratulierento congratulate
antwortento answer

Article in the dative:
masculinefeminineneuterplural
definitedemderdemden (+n)
indefiniteeinemeinereinem–

Examples:
Ich helfe dem Mann. (I'm helping the man.)
Das Buch gehört der Lehrerin. (The book belongs to the teacher.)
Die Suppe schmeckt den Kindern. (The soup tastes good to the children.)

explanation.en:
Verbs like geben, zeigen, schenken, bringen have two objects: the person is in the dative (To whom?), and the thing is in the accusative (What?).
Example: Ich gebe dem Kind (Dative) einen Ball (Accusative).

rule.en:
Structure: these verbs have two objects — the person in the Dativ (To whom?) and the thing in the Akkusativ (What?).

VerbMeaning
gebento give
zeigento show
schenkento give as a gift
bringento bring
erklärento explain
schreibento write

Order of objects:
two nounsdative before accusative
noun + pronounthe pronoun (whatever case) comes before the noun
two pronounsaccusative before dative

Examples:
Ich gebe dem Kind (dative) einen Ball (accusative). (I'm giving the child a ball.)
Ich gebe ihm (pronoun) einen Ball. (I'm giving him a ball.)
Ich gebe ihn (acc.) ihm (dat.). (I'm giving it to him.)

explanation.en:
Nine prepositions (e.g., in, auf, an, unter) change case: Where to? (movement/action) -> Accusative. Where? (location/rest) -> Dative.
Example: Ich hänge das Bild an die Wand (Acc.). Das Bild hängt an der Wand (Dat.).

rule.en:
The nine two-way prepositions: an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen.

QuestionCaseMeaning
Where to?Accusativemotion, direction, destination
Where?Dativeposition, rest, location

Rule of thumb: if something moves and its location changes → Accusative. If something stays/is at a location → Dative.

masculinefeminineneuter
Acc.dendiedas
Dat.demderdem

Examples:
Ich hänge das Bild an die Wand. (Acc. — motion, I'm hanging the picture)
Das Bild hängt an der Wand. (Dat. — position, the picture is hanging)
Ich gehe ins Kino. (I'm going to the cinema.) / Ich bin im Kino. (I'm at the cinema.)

explanation.en:
We use prepositions like zu, nach, in, an, über to describe directions. Zu is used for people or businesses (+ Dative), nach for cities and countries without articles.
Example: Ich gehe zum Arzt. Ich fliege nach Paris.

rule.en:
Key prepositions for direction:
PrepositionUse
zu (+ dative)to people, institutions, shops
nachto cities/countries without an article, cardinal directions
in (+ acc.)to countries with an article, enclosed spaces
an (+ acc.)to borders, shores, rivers
über (+ acc.)via a route/through a place

Contractions: zu + dem = zum, zu + der = zur, in + das = ins, an + das = ans.

Examples:
Ich gehe zum Arzt. (I'm going to the doctor.) Ich fliege nach Paris. (I'm flying to Paris.) Ich fahre in die Schweiz. (I'm going to Switzerland.) Wir fahren an den Rhein. (We're going to the Rhine.)

explanation.en:
Prepositions for points in time or duration: vor (past event), nach (after an event), seit (started in the past, still ongoing + Dative), für (for a duration + Accusative).
Example: Seit einem Jahr lerne ich Deutsch für einen Monat.

rule.en:
PrepositionCaseMeaning
vordativea point in the past (2 years ago)
nachdativeafter an event, afterward
seitdativestarted in the past, continues to now
füraccusativeplanned duration
bisaccusativeend point

seit vs. für: seit = the start of an action that's still going on today (use with the present tense!). für = a planned or completed duration.

Examples:
Seit einem Jahr lerne ich Deutsch. (I've been learning German for a year.)
Ich fahre für einen Monat nach Berlin. (I'm going to Berlin for a month.)
Vor zwei Jahren habe ich geheiratet. (I got married two years ago.)

title.en: Adjective endings after the indefinite/possessive article

explanation.en:
When a word like 'ein' or 'mein' comes before an adjective, the adjective in the nominative takes the gender signal: masculine (-er), neutral (-es), feminine (-e). In the accusative masculine, it is always -en.
Example: Das ist ein guter Mann. Ich habe ein schönes Auto.

rule.en:
Rule: after 'ein/mein/dein...', the adjective in the nominative and accusative (except masc. acc.) carries the gender signal that the article itself can't show.

masculinefeminineneuterplural
Nominative-er-e-es-en
Accusative-en-e-es-en
Dative-en-en-en-en

Rule of thumb: in the dative and plural it's almost always -en. Only in the nominative (and acc. feminine/neuter) do the endings differ by gender.

Examples:
Das ist ein guter Mann. (Nom. masc. — That's a good man.)
Ich habe ein schönes Auto. (Acc. neuter — I have a nice car.)
Ich habe einen guten Freund. (Acc. masc. — I have a good friend.)
Mit meinem neuen Auto. (Dative — With my new car.)

explanation.en:
We use Was für ein... to ask about characteristics or options (What kind of...?). The word 'ein' changes based on case and gender.
Example: Was für ein Auto hast du? (Neutral, Accusative).

rule.en:
Meaning: Was für ein...? asks about qualities, a type, or a choice (not about a specific quantity — 'welcher' is used for that).

Casemasculinefeminineneuterplural
Nominativewas für einwas für einewas für einwas für
Accusativewas für einenwas für einewas für einwas für

Note: 'für' has no influence on the case here — the case depends on the verb in the sentence!

Examples:
Was für ein Auto hast du? (Acc. neuter — What kind of car do you have?)
Was für eine Musik magst du? (What kind of music do you like?)
Was für Bücher liest du gern? (plural — What kind of books do you like to read?)

explanation.en:
The comparative form adds -er (often with an umlaut: alt -> älter). To show equality, use so ... wie. For differences, use the comparative + als.
Example: Er ist so groß wie ich. Er ist älter als ich.

rule.en:
Formation: adjective + -er (often with an umlaut for one-syllable words: a→ä, o→ö, u→ü).

Base formComparative
alt (old)älter
groß (big)größer
jung (young)jünger
gut (good)besser
gern (gladly)lieber
viel (much)mehr

Comparisons:
Equality(nicht) so ... wie (as ... as)
Differencecomparative + als (than)

Examples:
Er ist so groß wie ich. (He is as tall as me.)
Er ist älter als ich. (He is older than me.)
Ich arbeite mehr als er. (I work more than him.)

explanation.en:
The superlative is the highest form. After verbs, we usually use am ...-sten. Before nouns, we use the definite article + -ste with correct adjective ending.
Example: Kaffee schmeckt mir am besten. Das ist das schönste Haus.

rule.en:
Two forms:
After verbs (predicative)am + adjective + -sten
Before nouns (attributive)definite article + adjective + -ste + ending

Base formComparativeSuperlative (am ...)
altälteram ältesten
großgrößeram größten
gutbesseram besten
gernlieberam liebsten
vielmehram meisten

Note: adjectives ending in -d, -t, -s, -z, -sch get an extra -e- (am kältesten, am heißesten).

Examples:
Kaffee schmeckt mir am besten. (I like the taste of coffee the most.)
Das ist das schönste Haus der Stadt. (That's the most beautiful house in the city.)

explanation.en:
We use dieser, diese, dieses to point out a specific person or object (this). They decline exactly like definite articles (der, die, das).
Example: Mir gefällt dieses Buch (Buch is neutral -> dieses).

rule.en:
Declension: dieser, diese, dieses is declined exactly like the definite article (der, die, das).

masculinefeminineneuterplural
Nominativedieserdiesediesesdiese
Accusativediesendiesediesesdiese
Dativediesemdieserdiesemdiesen

Compare with the article: der→dieser, die→diese, das→dieses, dem→diesem, den→diesen.

Examples:
Mir gefällt dieses Buch. (Nom./Acc. neuter — I like this book.)
Diese Wohnung ist teuer. (This apartment is expensive.)
Ich helfe diesem Mann. (Dative — I'm helping this man.)

explanation.en:
For extra polite requests, we use Subjunctive II. Mostly we use hätte, wäre or the combination würde + infinitive at the end.
Example: Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee. Würden Sie mir bitte helfen?

rule.en:
Formation with würde: würde (conjugated) + subject ... + infinitive at the end.

ichwürde
duwürdest
er/sie/eswürde
wirwürden
ihrwürdet
sie/Siewürden

Important fixed forms (without würde):
habenhätte, hättest, hätte, hätten, hättet, hätten
seinwäre, wärst, wäre, wären, wärt, wären
könnenkönnte, könntest, könnte, könnten, könntet, könnten

Examples:
Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee. (I'd like a coffee.)
Würden Sie mir bitte helfen? (Would you please help me?)
Könntest du bitte das Fenster schließen? (Could you please close the window?)

explanation.en:
Personal pronouns change depending on the case: Nominative (ich/du), Accusative (mich/dich), and Dative (mir/dir).
Example: Hilfst du mir (Dative)? Ich liebe dich (Accusative).

rule.en:
Declension of personal pronouns:

NominativeAccusativeDative
ichmichmir
dudichdir
erihnihm
siesieihr
esesihm
wirunsuns
ihreucheuch
sie/Siesie/Sieihnen/Ihnen

Which case, and when? Accusative after verbs with a direct object (lieben, sehen, kennen). Dative after verbs answering 'To whom?' (helfen, danken, gefallen).

Examples:
Hilfst du mir? (Dative — Will you help me?)
Ich liebe dich. (Accusative — I love you.)
Kennst du ihn? (Do you know him?)

explanation.en:
Reflexive verbs require a reflexive pronoun (e.g., mich, dich, sich). It shows that the action reflects back to the subject.
Example: Ich wasche mich. Er freut sich.

rule.en:
Declension of reflexive pronouns in the accusative:

ichmich
dudich
er/sie/essich
wiruns
ihreuch
sie/Siesich

Note: only 'er/sie/es' and 'sie/Sie' have the form sich. For the other persons, the reflexive pronouns are identical to the accusative pronouns (mich, dich, uns, euch).

Important reflexive verbs: sich waschen (to wash oneself), sich freuen auf/über (to look forward to/be happy about), sich interessieren für (to be interested in), sich beeilen (to hurry), sich erinnern an (to remember), sich fühlen (to feel).

Examples:
Ich wasche mich jeden Morgen. (I wash myself every morning.)
Er freut sich auf die Ferien. (He's looking forward to the vacation.)
Wir beeilen uns. (We're hurrying.)

explanation.en:
Many verbs have a fixed preposition and a fixed case. You have to memorize them together. Key examples: warten auf (+ Accusative), sprechen mit (+ Dative).
Example: Ich warte auf den Bus.

rule.en:
Principle: some verbs always need the same preposition + a fixed case — this combination has to be memorized.

Verb + prepositionCase
warten auf (to wait for)accusative
sich freuen auf (to look forward to)accusative
sich interessieren für (to be interested in)accusative
denken an (to think of)accusative
sprechen mit (to talk to)dative
sich treffen mit (to meet with)dative
Angst haben vor (to be afraid of)dative

Asking about them: for people you ask Auf wen?/Mit wem? (For whom?/With whom?), for things Worauf?/Womit? (wo(r) + preposition).

Examples:
Ich warte auf den Bus. (I'm waiting for the bus.)
Ich spreche mit meiner Mutter. (I'm talking with my mother.)
Worauf wartest du? — Auf den Bus. (What are you waiting for? — For the bus.)

explanation.en:
Deshalb expresses a consequence (therefore / that's why). Note: deshalb takes the 1st position in the main clause, followed immediately by the conjugated verb!
Example: Ich bin krank, deshalb bleibe ich im Bett.

rule.en:
Position: deshalb is an adverb (not a connector like 'weil') and takes position 1 in the main clause. Right after it comes the conjugated verb (position 2), then the subject.

Position 1Position 2 (verb)SubjectRest
Deshalbbleibeichim Bett.

Comparison with weil:
weilsubordinate clause, verb at the end: ..., weil ich krank bin.
deshalbtwo main clauses: Ich bin krank, deshalb bleibe ich im Bett.

Similar words: deswegen, darum, daher (same position and meaning).

Example: Ich bin krank, deshalb bleibe ich im Bett. (I'm sick, so I'm staying in bed.)

title.en: Subjunctive II: asking, requesting and giving advice politely

explanation.en:
In module A2.2 we expand Subjunctive II. We use sollte to give advice and könnte to ask very politely.
Example: Du solltest zum Arzt gehen. Könnten Sie das Fenster schließen?

rule.en:
Extending the Konjunktiv II:
FormFunctionExample
solltegiving adviceDu solltest mehr schlafen. (You should sleep more.)
könntea very polite question / suggestionKönntest du mir helfen? (Could you help me?)
hätte/wärea wishIch hätte gern Zeit. (I'd like to have time.)

Conjugation of sollen: ich sollte, du solltest, er/sie/es sollte, wir sollten, ihr solltet, sie/Sie sollten.

Examples:
Du solltest zum Arzt gehen. (advice — You should go to the doctor.)
Könnten Sie das Fenster schließen? (polite request — Could you close the window?)

title.en: Adjective endings after the definite article

explanation.en:
After the definite article (der, die, das), adjectives in the nominative always end in -e. In the plural and other cases (Dative, Accusative masculine), the ending is mostly -en.
Example: Der neue Kollege ist nett. Ich helfe dem alten Mann.

rule.en:
Rule: after the definite article, the article itself already shows the gender — so the adjective usually takes a 'weak' ending.

masculinefeminineneuterplural
Nominative-e-e-e-en
Accusative-en-e-e-en
Dative-en-en-en-en

Rule of thumb: only in the nominative (all genders) and accusative (feminine/neuter) is it -e. In all other cases: -en.

Examples:
Der neue Kollege ist nett. (Nom. masc. — The new colleague is nice.)
Ich helfe dem alten Mann. (Dative — I'm helping the old man.)
Ich kenne die neue Kollegin. (Acc. fem. — I know the new colleague.)

title.en: Relative clause with relative pronoun in the nominative

explanation.en:
A relative clause describes a noun in more detail. In the nominative, the relative pronoun looks exactly like the definite article (der, die, das, die). The verb goes to the end.
Example: Das ist der Mann, der hier wohnt.

rule.en:
Relative pronoun in the nominative = like the definite article:
masculinefeminineneuterplural
derdiedasdie

Rule: the gender of the relative pronoun matches the noun it refers to, while the case depends on its function in the subordinate clause. The verb goes at the end.

Structure: main clause + noun, + relative pronoun + ... + verb.

Examples:
Das ist der Mann, der hier wohnt. (Mann = masculine — That's the man who lives here.)
Das ist die Frau, die Deutsch unterrichtet. (Frau = feminine — That's the woman who teaches German.)
Das ist das Kind, das gern spielt. (Kind = neuter — That's the child who likes to play.)

explanation.en:
The verb werden means a change or development (to become). It is irregular: ich werde, du wirst, er/sie/es wird.
Example: Mein Sohn wird bald Arzt. Es wird kalt.

rule.en:
Present tense conjugation (irregular):

ichwerde
duwirst
er/sie/eswird
wirwerden
ihrwerdet
sie/Siewerden

Three uses:
1. Change of state+ adjective: Es wird kalt. (It's getting cold.)
2. Profession/state+ noun: Er wird Arzt. (He's going to be a doctor.)
3. Future I+ infinitive at the end: Ich werde morgen kommen. (I will come tomorrow.)

Examples:
Mein Sohn wird bald Arzt. (My son will soon be a doctor.)
Es wird dunkel. (It's getting dark.)
Ich werde dich anrufen. (I will call you.)

title.en: The verb lassen (to let / have something done)

explanation.en:
The verb lassen has two main meanings: to leave something somewhere, or to have something done by someone else. Lassen is in position 2, the main verb is at the end.
Example: Ich lasse mein Auto reparieren (The mechanic does it).

rule.en:
Conjugation (irregular): ich lasse, du lässt, er/sie/es lässt, wir lassen, ihr lasst, sie/Sie lassen.

Two meanings:
1. to leave (behind)to leave something somewhere: Ich lasse das Auto zu Hause. (I'm leaving the car at home.)
2. to have (something) doneto have someone else do an action: Ich lasse mein Auto reparieren. (I'm having my car repaired.)

Word order: lassen in position 2, the second verb's infinitive right at the end.

Examples:
Ich lasse meinen Schlüssel im Büro. (I'm leaving my key at the office.)
Ich lasse mir die Haare schneiden. (I'm getting my hair cut.)

explanation.en:
We use damit to express a purpose or goal (What for?). The conjugated verb goes to the end. Note: The subjects in the main and subordinate clause are usually different.
Example: Ich gebe dir Geld, damit du ein Buch kaufst.

rule.en:
Use: damit expresses a goal/intention (What for? For what purpose?). Important: the subjects of the main and subordinate clauses are usually different.

Word order: main clause, + damit + subject + ... + verb (end).

ConnectorWhen to use it
damittwo different subjects
um ... zuthe same subject in both clauses (+ infinitive, no separate verb)

Examples:
Ich gebe dir Geld, damit du ein Buch kaufst. (ich ≠ du — I'm giving you money so you can buy a book.)
Compare: Ich lerne Deutsch, um einen Job zu finden. (same subject: ich — I'm learning German to find a job.)

title.en: Indirect question with a question word

explanation.en:
An indirect question is more polite. We start with a phrase like 'Können Sie mir sagen...' and connect it with the question word (wann, wo, wie). The verb goes to the end.
Example: Können Sie mir sagen, wo der Bahnhof ist?

rule.en:
Structure: polite introduction (Können Sie mir sagen...? / Ich weiß nicht,...) + question word + subject + ... + verb (end).

Direct questionIndirect question
Wo ist der Bahnhof?Können Sie mir sagen, wo der Bahnhof ist?
Wann kommt der Zug?Wissen Sie, wann der Zug kommt?

Typical introductions: Können Sie mir sagen...? (Can you tell me...?) Wissen Sie...? (Do you know...?) Ich möchte wissen,... (I'd like to know...) Ich weiß nicht,... (I don't know...)

Examples:
Können Sie mir sagen, wo der Bahnhof ist? (Can you tell me where the station is?)
Ich weiß nicht, wie das funktioniert. (I don't know how this works.)

explanation.en:
If a direct question is a Yes/No question (no question word), we use ob (whether/if) to form the indirect question. The verb moves to the end.
Example: Ich weiß nicht, ob er heute kommt.

rule.en:
Structure: polite introduction + ob + subject + ... + verb (end). Used when the direct question has no question word (a yes/no question).

Direct question (yes/no)Indirect question with ob
Kommt er heute?Ich weiß nicht, ob er heute kommt.
Hast du Zeit?Ich frage mich, ob du Zeit hast.

Difference from question-word questions: with W-questions (wo, wann, wie...) the question word stays; with yes/no questions, ob (whether/if) replaces the missing question word.

Example: Ich weiß nicht, ob er heute kommt. (I don't know whether he's coming today.)

title.en: Review: prepositions with accusative and dative

explanation.en:
Review of two-way prepositions: movement/direction requires the Accusative (Where to?), while fixed location/rest requires the Dative (Where?).
Example: Stell das Glas auf den Tisch (Acc.). Das Glas steht auf dem Tisch (Dat.).

rule.en:
Summary of the nine two-way prepositions: an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen.

QuestionCase
Where to? (motion)Accusative
Where? (position)Dative

Quick test: if you can answer with 'Where is something moving to?' → Accusative. If you can answer with 'Where is it located?' → Dative.

Examples:
Stell das Glas auf den Tisch. (Acc. — motion: I'm putting it there)
Das Glas steht auf dem Tisch. (Dat. — position: it's already standing there)
Ich lege das Buch in die Tasche. (I'm putting the book in the bag.) / Das Buch liegt in der Tasche. (The book is lying in the bag.)

explanation.en: Review of pronouns for people. Accusative (Who/What? -> <g>mich, dich, ihn...</g>) and Dative (To whom? -> <g>mir, dir, ihm...</g>).

rule.en:
Summary:
NominativeAccusativeDative
ichmichmir
dudichdir
erihnihm
siesieihr
esesihm
wirunsuns
ihreucheuch
sie/Siesie/Sieihnen/Ihnen

Rule of thumb: Accusative = Whom/What? (direct object). Dative = To whom? (indirect object).

Examples:
Ich sehe ihn. (Acc. — I see him.)
Ich gebe ihm das Buch. (Dative — I'm giving him the book.)

explanation.en:
Review of sentence structure: In subordinate clauses with connectors like weil, dass, wenn, the conjugated verb always moves to the very end of the clause.
Example: Ich denke, dass das wichtig ist.

rule.en:
Summary of the main connectors:
ConnectorMeaning
weilreason (why?)
dasscontent/object (what?)
wenncondition/repetition
obindirect yes/no question
damitgoal/purpose

Shared rule: in all subordinate clauses with these connectors, the conjugated verb goes right to the end of the sentence.

Examples:
Ich denke, dass das wichtig ist. (I think that's important.)
Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin. (I'm staying home because I'm sick.)
Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt. (I don't know if he's coming.)

title.en: Review: adjective endings after the indefinite article

explanation.en:
Review: After 'ein/mein', the adjective in the nominative carries the gender signal: -er (masc.), -es (neutral), -e (fem.). In the accusative masculine, it takes -en.
Example: ein alter Freund.

rule.en:
Summary of endings after 'ein/mein/dein...':
masculinefeminineneuterplural
Nominative-er-e-es-en
Accusative-en-e-es-en
Dative-en-en-en-en

Rule of thumb: only in the nominative does the adjective clearly show the gender (-er/-e/-es), because 'ein' itself gives no signal. In all other cases: mostly -en.

Examples:
ein alter Freund. (Nom. masc. — an old friend.)
eine alte Freundin. (Nom. fem. — an old friend, female.)
mit einem alten Freund. (Dative — with an old friend.)

explanation.en:
Review: The conjunction dass introduces a subordinate object clause. The verb goes to the end. Often used after expressions like: Ich finde, dass... / Es ist gut, dass...
Example: Es ist gut, dass du hier bist.

rule.en:
Summary: dass introduces a subordinate clause, the conjugated verb goes at the end. Often used after expressions of opinion and feeling.

ExpressionExample
Ich finde, dass... (I think that...)Ich finde, dass das gut ist.
Es ist gut/schön, dass... (It's good/nice that...)Es ist gut, dass du hier bist.
Ich hoffe, dass... (I hope that...)Ich hoffe, dass es klappt.

Note: with two verbs (modal verb, Perfekt), both go to the end, with the conjugated verb last: Ich finde, dass er das gut gemacht hat.

Example: Es ist gut, dass du hier bist. (It's good that you're here.)
